description: En la escala Bortle, 1 es el cielo más oscuro de la Tierra; un "Bortle Cero" sería aún más limpio, como el que ve SPHEREx desde el espacio. Vamos por Planet X and SPHEREx en la sede CUGDL: una web pública donde cualquiera escribe unas coordenadas y ve cómo cambia ese pedazo de cielo. Soy Miguel, desarrollador web y divulgador del cielo (observatorio.bortlecero.com). Buscamos a alguien con Python/Astropy o análisis de datos y a alguien de física o astronomía. Ganas de aprender, bienvenidas.
summary:
Starphere (live at https://starphere-earth-hosting.web.app/) is an open-source, public web blink comparator built for NASA’s Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Visitors can enter any RA / Dec coordinates, search by object name via SIMBAD/Sesame, or select one of five official benchmark targets to explore an interactive all-sky WebGL viewer and inspect multi-epoch NASA SPHEREx near-infrared cutouts (0.75–5.0 µm) fetched live from NASA/IPAC IRSA.

A naive blink of raw SPHEREx frames breaks because the spacecraft rotates 180° between passes, each exposure samples a different wavelength across the Linear Variable Filter, and bright stars saturate. Our Python/FastAPI ingestion pipeline automatically subtracts zodiacal light (ZODI), masks detector quality flags (FLAGS), reprojects every frame onto a common North-up WCS grid, groups exposures by spectral band, and propagates Gaia DR3 proper motion and parallax to each exposure date. For ultra-faint targets like WISE 0855−0714, a "comet-mode" deep stack co-adds frames along the predicted motion.

By turning complex Level 2b FITS data into an accessible, scientifically validated blink tool, Starphere empowers researchers, citizen scientists, and the public to spot moving brown dwarfs, variable stars, and potential Planet X candidates.

1. Interactive All-Sky Explorer (mockup/):

- Opens on a full-screen, dependency-free WebGL 2 sky sphere built with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

- Displays three custom all-sky layers generated from NASA SVS Deep Star Maps 2020 (visible light) and IRSA’s SPHEREx DR1 all-sky cube (4.77 µm and false-color RGB), plus an optional celestial coordinate grid.

- Users can pan/zoom across the sky, pick any of the five challenge benchmarks (Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae, R Draconis), resolve object names through Harvard’s SIMBAD/Sesame mirror, or enter custom RA / Dec coordinates.

2. Live NASA/IRSA Data Ingestion (src/spherex_ingest/):

- A FastAPI backend queries IRSA’s SIAv2 service (spherex_dr1, spherex_qr3, spherex_dr1_deep, spherex_qr3_deep) and downloads Level 2b Multi-Extension FITS cutouts (IMAGE, FLAGS, VARIANCE, ZODI, EPSF, WCS-WAVE).

- Long-running queries run asynchronously via a bounded job queue (Cloud Tasks + Firestore in Google Cloud Run; SQLite + thread pool locally), while the UI displays live progress through the data’s journey from star to telescope to screen.

3. Science-Ready Blink & Deep Stack:

- Alignment & Cleaning: Subtracts the ZODI zodiacal background, applies FLAGS bitmasks (handling saturation, BLOOM, OVERFLOW, and transients), and reprojects rotated frames (SPS_EPA 180° flips) onto a unified North-up TAN grid.

- Spectral Band Grouping: Evaluates local wavelength at the target pixel via WCS-WAVE and groups frames into SPHEREx Bands 1–6 (defaulting to Band 6, 4.42–5.00 µm, closest to WISE W2).

- Gaia DR3 Verification: Propagates proper motion and trigonometric parallax to each exposure’s MJD-AVG and compares against sub-pixel centroids measured with photutils.

- Comet-Mode Deep Stack: Shifts and co-adds usable exposures along the target’s predicted trajectory to reduce noise by ~√N and reveal faint sources invisible in single frames (such as WISE 0855−0714), accessible via a Single frames | Stack of N toggle.

- Basic & Advanced Views + Sky Guide: Offers an approachable Basic mode, an Advanced mode (with difference maps ΔI, release tags, position angles, filter half-widths, and scientific caveats), a guided tour, and an optional Gemini-powered Sky Guide (POST /api/v1/assistant).

Benefits & Intended Impact

- Scientific Validity Without Barriers: Anyone—from professional astronomers to Backyard Worlds citizen scientists and students—can inspect real SPHEREx cutouts in a browser without downloading ~62–72 MB detector FITS files or writing Astropy/WCS reprojection scripts.

- Prevents Common Misinterpretations: By separating spectral bands, flagging saturated cores, and displaying Gaia-propagated positions alongside clear caveats, the tool helps users distinguish real motion or variability from instrumental and chromatic effects.

- Open & Reusable: Released under Apache 2.0, both the modular ingestion engine and the zero-build frontend can be extended for future SPHEREx data releases and citizen-science campaigns.

Tools, Languages, Software & Infrastructure

- Backend & Science Pipeline: Python 3.12+ (managed with Astral uv), FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, Astropy, reproject, PyVO, Photutils, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, HTTPX.

- Frontend: Vanilla HTML5, CSS3, ES6+ JavaScript, WebGL 2 (custom sky-sphere shader), IndexedDB (client-side bundle caching).

- AI Assistant: Google Gemini API (gemini-3.5-flash-lite via REST) for the optional Sky Guide.

- Cloud, Testing & CI/CD: Docker, Google Cloud Run, Google Cloud Storage, Firestore, Cloud Tasks, Firebase Hosting, GitHub Actions (Workload Identity Federation), Pytest, Ruff, and Playwright (Chromium browser tests).

- Hardware: Standard consumer laptops (Linux and Windows) for development and serverless cloud infrastructure (Google Cloud Run) for public hosting.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered

- Astrophotography-Inspired "Comet Mode" Stack: Instead of stopping at single-frame blinking—where ultra-cold brown dwarfs like WISE 0855−0714 remain undetected—the team implemented a motion-compensated deep stack with explicit flux-mixing caveats.

- Dual-Audience Design: The interface pairs a cinematic "inside-the-sky" WebGL explorer with a Basic / Advanced toggle so newcomers aren't overwhelmed while astronomers still get difference maps, WCS diagnostics, and Gaia residuals.

- Resilience & Cost Control: Because IRSA cutouts lack CORS headers and can take 30–70+ seconds to fetch and align, the team built a server-side proxy with admission limits (max 6 new jobs/min, 8 outstanding), deduplication, Cloud Storage result caching, and IndexedDB browser caching.

- Real-World Service Constraints: With CDS Strasbourg services unavailable during the hackathon, the team routed object resolution through Harvard’s SIMBAD/Sesame mirror and self-hosted pre-rendered all-sky WebP maps so the sky explorer loads fast and reliably.
